# PRD: Hiring Ascent — End-to-End Hiring Platform

## 0. Document Purpose

This PRD defines the v1 scope for an internal hiring platform that tracks recruitment end-to-end — from requisition open through candidate submission, interviews, and onboarding — across both internal HR/referral channels and external partner agencies. It is written for the PM, engineering, and downstream UX/architecture owners. It builds on a prior brainstorming session (`brainstorm-intent.md`, referenced throughout this doc's memlog) and does not duplicate that material. Features are grouped with Functional Requirements (FRs) nested underneath; unresolved items are tagged inline as `[ASSUMPTION]` and indexed in §10.

## 1. Vision

Today, recruitment at the organization runs through disconnected channels — agency emails, informal employee referrals, ad-hoc spreadsheets — with no shared source of truth. Two agencies can independently submit the same candidate and both believe they're owed credit. Leadership has no reliable signal of which teams are struggling to hire versus coasting. Hiring managers only find out an interview happened after the fact, if at all.

Hiring Ascent is the organization's single system of record for recruitment: every requisition gets a Role ID, every candidate submitted against it is deduplicated and tracked through a hiring-manager-defined interview pipeline, and every stakeholder — internal HR, hiring managers, and partner agencies — sees the slice of that record relevant to them. It replaces disconnected, dispute-prone channels with one shared, auditable pipeline, and it starts turning "who's ever filled this seat" into institutional memory instead of tribal knowledge.

## 2. Scope at a Glance (v1)

The `[Must]` / `[Should]` tag (also on each FR heading in §5) carries the original stakeholder prioritization forward: **Must** is the non-negotiable core — cutting it defeats the product's purpose. **Should** is fully committed for v1 but is where scope would flex first under real timeline pressure. (What's explicitly deferred past v1 is in §7 Out of Scope for MVP.)

## 3. Target User

### 3.1 Jobs To Be Done

- **Internal HR** — see every candidate against a role regardless of source, resolve identity conflicts fairly, keep the requisition lifecycle (open → filled → closed) accurate.
- **Hiring managers** — see who's actually in the pipeline for their role, control how many interview rounds it takes to hire, know who's interviewing and when, without chasing HR or agencies for status.
- **External agency recruiters** — know which roles they're allowed to work, avoid wasted effort submitting a candidate someone already put forward, get credited and paid without a dispute, prove their track record.
- **Employee referrers** — get their informally-vetted referral into the same pipeline as any other candidate, and find out what happened to it. Referrals carry an inherent trust signal — someone inside the org has already vetted the person informally — which is expected to make them convert at a higher rate than cold agency/direct submissions; the platform should give referrals full pipeline parity, not second-class treatment, on the strength of that signal.
- **Org leadership (managers of managers)** — get a rolled-up, bottoms-up signal of recruitment health without asking every team individually.

### 3.2 Non-Users (v1)

- **Candidates** are explicitly not platform users in v1 — no candidate accounts, login, or self-service status (see §6 Non-Goals).

### 3.3 Key User Journeys

*Employee referrers don't get a dedicated journey below: their submission flow mirrors UJ-1 (minus the pre-check-as-competitive-edge framing, since they aren't racing an agency), and their status-checking experience is FR-17's portal view, authenticated via company SSO. Called out explicitly here so the omission reads as a choice, not a gap.*

- **UJ-1. Amara submits a candidate without wasting her afternoon.**
  - **Persona + context:** Amara is a recruiter at a partner agency the organization has enabled for a "Senior Backend Engineer" role.
  - **Entry state:** Authenticated as an agency recruiter (invited by her agency's admin). Lands on her agency's dashboard showing only roles enabled for her agency.
  - **Path:** She opens the role, reads the JD to confirm fit, and before writing up her candidate's profile, runs the pre-check (email/phone) to confirm no one has already submitted this person for this role. Pre-check comes back clear. She uploads the candidate's resume and details against the Role ID.
  - **Climax:** The submission succeeds and lands in the role's pipeline at its first Interview Level, timestamped — her proof of first submission.
  - **Resolution:** She sees the candidate listed on her own view of the role's pipeline. She'll check back via the portal for status; no email push happens unless an interview gets scheduled.
  - **Edge case:** If pre-check finds a match, she sees "already submitted" instead of being allowed to duplicate the effort.

- **UJ-2. Priya (Internal HR) resolves a submission conflict without playing judge from scratch.**
  - **Persona + context:** Priya is Internal HR/Talent Acquisition (TA), managing five open roles across two teams.
  - **Entry state:** Authenticated via company SSO. Opens the per-role dashboard for "Senior Backend Engineer."
  - **Path:** She sees every candidate submitted against the role — agency, referral, and direct — each tagged with its source. Two submissions for the same person landed forty minutes apart; the platform already resolved it (first-in kept, second flagged) and shows both agencies the timestamp gap.
  - **Climax:** Because the timestamp record is visible to both submitters, Priya doesn't have to personally mediate a dispute — the audit trail already answered the "who was first" question.
  - **Resolution:** She moves on to reviewing the rest of the pipeline instead of firefighting a credit dispute.

- **UJ-3. Marcus (hiring manager) sets up his pipeline once and stops chasing status.**
  - **Persona + context:** Marcus is hiring for "Senior Backend Engineer" and doesn't post the requisition himself — HR does — but he owns the outcome.
  - **Entry state:** Authenticated via SSO. Opens his role's dashboard.
  - **Path:** He sets the role to require 3 interview levels (Screen → Technical → Final) and assigns an interviewer pool to each level. As candidates arrive, he sees all of them — agency, referral, HR-direct — with who submitted each one. He picks an interviewer from the Technical pool and the recruiter (HR or agency) schedules the interview against that assignment.
  - **Climax:** When the interview is logged, Marcus is notified of the interviewer's name and time — he learns it happened without asking anyone. After it happens, the interviewer submits ratings, notes, and a verdict; Marcus reviews that feedback and decides himself whether the candidate moves to Final.
  - **Resolution:** Every candidate for this role moves through the same 3 levels with a real decision at each one, so Marcus is comparing like with like by the time he makes an offer decision — and he made every advancement call himself, not a scoring rule.

- **UJ-4. Diane sees a closed requisition become something she can actually act on.**
  - **Persona + context:** Diane is a director two levels above Marcus, reviewing hiring health for the quarter.
  - **Entry state:** Authenticated via SSO, viewing a rolled-up health dashboard covering all teams under them.
  - **Path:** They see time-to-fill, aging requisitions, pipeline volume, and offer-accept rate aggregated bottoms-up from each team. When "Senior Backend Engineer" closes with a hire, it converts into a position record tied to that employee.
  - **Climax:** They see, at a glance, which teams have requisitions aging past a healthy threshold, without messaging every manager individually.
  - **Resolution:** Over time, if that seat opens again, it reopens as a known position rather than a brand-new requisition — building a real headcount history, not just a hiring funnel snapshot.

## 4. Glossary

- **Requisition** — A request to fill a position, identified by a **Role ID**. Has a lifecycle: open → in-progress → filled/closed. Defines its own **Interview Pipeline**.
- **Role ID** — The unique identifier for a requisition. All **Candidates**, submissions, and interview activity nest under it.
- **Candidate** — A person submitted against a Role ID, identified by a **Candidate ID**. Deduplicated per Role ID across sources.
- **Submission** — The act of an internal HR user, hiring manager (indirectly), or agency recruiter putting a Candidate forward for a Role ID. Each Submission has a **Source** and a timestamp.
- **Source** — The origin of a Submission: `internal-hr`, `employee-referral`, or `agency` (with the specific **Agency** identified).
- **Agency** — A partner recruiting firm, onboarded at the org level, with one or more **Agency Recruiters** invited by its own admin.
- **Agency Recruiter** — A user belonging to an Agency, scoped to only the Roles explicitly enabled for that Agency.
- **Dedup** — The enforced, blocking identity-matching process (FR-2; by email/phone/resume-hash in v1) that prevents duplicate Candidate Submissions for the same Role ID. First Submission is kept; later ones are flagged.
- **Pre-Check** — The advisory, non-blocking query (FR-3) a recruiter can run before completing a full Submission, to check whether a Candidate is already in the pipeline for a Role ID. Distinct from Dedup: Pre-Check informs, Dedup enforces.
- **Candidate Status** — A Candidate's state within a Role ID's pipeline: `Active` (default, in-progress), `Rejected`, `Withdrawn`, or `Hired` (FR-18, FR-25).
- **Interview Pipeline** — The ordered set of Interview Levels defined per Role ID by the Hiring Manager. Every Candidate under that Role ID progresses through the same levels.
- **Interview Level** — A single stage in a Role's Interview Pipeline (e.g., Screen, Technical, Final), with an associated **Interviewer Pool**.
- **Interviewer Pool** — The set of people approved to interview at a given Interview Level for a Role.
- **Position Record** — The persistent record a Requisition converts into once filled, tied to the hired employee, enabling reopen-on-attrition instead of fresh-requisition-from-scratch.
- **Recruitment Health** — The rolled-up metric set (time-to-fill, aging requisitions, pipeline volume, offer-accept rate) aggregated bottoms-up through the org hierarchy.
- **Agency Scorecard** — The per-Agency funnel view: Candidates referred → progressed per Interview Level → joined.

## Cross-Cutting NFRs

- **One canonical data model per concept, projected into audience-specific views — not bespoke per-stakeholder features.** This is a governing design principle, not just a dashboard detail: it applies to the Interview Pipeline (§5.4), the Agency Scorecard (§5.9), and the Requisition/Position Record (§5.7), not only the per-role dashboard (FR-10 is one instance of it). When any of these later needs a second audience-specific cut, the correct move is another projection of the same underlying model — never a parallel, bespoke feature built to serve just that audience.
- **Access control is the load-bearing security property**, enforced at the data layer, not just hidden in UI — see FR-5, FR-7 for the specific Agency-isolation guarantees.
- **Dedup must be synchronous, immutable, and use a server-side authoritative timestamp** (never client-supplied), with a monotonic sequence ID breaking any true simultaneous-timestamp collision — see FR-2, FR-4 for the full acceptance criteria.
- **Availability expectation:** business-hours reliability appropriate to an internal tool partner agencies depend on for their livelihood (a missed submission window has a real financial consequence for an agency) — no formal SLA defined in v1 `[ASSUMPTION]`, see Open Questions.

## Constraints and Guardrails

**Privacy**
- Candidate PII (resume, contact details) is scoped per Role ID and per authorized viewer (Internal HR, the relevant Hiring Manager, and the submitting Agency/referrer only).
- No candidate accounts or consent-management flows exist in v1 since candidates are non-users (§6); data handling is entirely on behalf of the organization and its agencies, which raises a retention-policy question — see Open Question 4.

**Integration and Dependencies**
- Internal HR, Hiring Managers, and employee referrers all authenticate via company SSO — referrers are internal org members, not external partners, so no separate onboarding flow exists for them. `[ASSUMPTION]` Specific SSO provider unconfirmed — see Open Question 2.
- Agencies are onboarded via a one-time, internal-HR-driven agency setup; the agency's own admin then invites its recruiters. No self-service agency registration.
- Outbound email is required for candidate interview logistics (FR-16). `[ASSUMPTION]` No existing email/transactional-messaging provider specified — see Open Question 3.
- `[ASSUMPTION]` No existing Human Resources Information System (HRIS) or Applicant Tracking System (ATS) integration is assumed required for v1; Hiring Ascent is standalone aside from SSO and email.

## 5. Features

### 5.1 Requisition & Candidate Identity

**Description:** The structural foundation of the platform. Every requisition is a Role ID; every candidate submitted against it is deduplicated at the point of submission, not after. This surfaced independently across three separate design discussions and is treated as the non-negotiable core the rest of the system depends on.

**Functional Requirements:**

#### FR-1: Create and identify requisitions by Role ID `[Must]`
Internal HR can open a new requisition, which is assigned a unique Role ID and an associated job description (JD).

**Consequences (testable):**
- Every requisition has exactly one Role ID, generated at creation, immutable thereafter.
- A JD is required before a requisition can be enabled for any agency (blocks FR-5).

#### FR-2: Deduplicate candidate submissions per role `[Must]`
The system deduplicates Candidate Submissions against a given Role ID by email, phone, and resume-hash. Realizes UJ-1, UJ-2.

**Consequences (testable):**
- A second Submission matching an existing Candidate's email, phone, or resume-hash for the same Role ID is rejected as a duplicate and flagged "already in pipeline" instead of creating a second Candidate record.
- A resume-hash match alone does not auto-reject — it must be corroborated by a matching email or phone before a Submission is rejected as a duplicate, to guard against hash collisions between two distinct candidates.
- The original (first-timestamped) Submission is the one that proceeds through the pipeline. Timestamps are recorded by a single server-side authoritative clock (never client-supplied); if two Submissions record identical server timestamps, a monotonic sequence ID breaks the tie deterministically. See Cross-Cutting NFRs.
- `[ASSUMPTION]` Exact-match dedup (email/phone/resume-hash) is sufficient for v1; fuzzy matching (name variants, resume-content similarity) is deferred — see §7.

#### FR-3: Pre-check before full submission `[Should]`
Any recruiter (Internal HR or Agency) can query whether a candidate (by email/phone) is already submitted against a specific Role ID *before* completing a full profile write-up. Realizes UJ-1.

**Consequences (testable):**
- Pre-check returns a clear match/no-match result without exposing the other submitter's identity or submission content.
- Pre-check is available on the role page before the upload form is completed.
- Pre-check is advisory, not a lock: the system re-verifies at actual submission time (FR-2), and if a competing Submission completed in between, the submitter sees a distinct "no longer clear" message rather than a generic rejection.

#### FR-4: Timestamped audit trail for submission disputes `[Should]`
Every Submission (including rejected duplicates) is timestamped and the record is visible to both the accepted and the flagged submitter. Realizes UJ-2.

**Consequences (testable):**
- A flagged (duplicate) submitter sees the exact time gap between their submission and the accepted one, computed from the server-side authoritative timestamp (see FR-2, Cross-Cutting NFRs) — never a client-supplied one.
- Audit records are immutable once created.

**Feature-specific NFRs:**
- Dedup check must complete synchronously before a submission is accepted or rejected — no eventual-consistency window where two duplicate Candidates can both exist.

### 5.2 Agency Access & Candidate Submission

**Description:** Controls what an external Agency Recruiter can see and do, scoped strictly to roles their agency has been enabled for.

**Functional Requirements:**

#### FR-5: Role-based visibility for agencies `[Must]`
An Agency Recruiter can see only the Roles explicitly enabled for their Agency. Realizes UJ-1.

**Consequences (testable):**
- Roles not enabled for an Agency do not appear in that Agency's role list, JD, or any candidate data — not just hidden in the UI, but unreachable via direct access too.
- Enabling/disabling a Role for an Agency is an internal-HR action.
- `[ASSUMPTION]` Disabling is forward-only: it blocks new Submissions from that Agency for that Role, but does not remove, freeze, or otherwise affect that Agency's Candidates already in the pipeline — they continue through their Interview Levels normally.

#### FR-6: JD review before submission `[Must]`
An Agency Recruiter can view the full JD for any Role enabled for their Agency before submitting a candidate. Realizes UJ-1.

**Consequences (testable):**
- The JD version an Agency Recruiter reviewed is snapshotted against their Submission, so a later JD edit by HR does not retroactively change what an already-submitted Candidate was evaluated against.

#### FR-7: Candidate submission with resume `[Must]`
An Agency Recruiter can submit a Candidate against an enabled Role, including resume upload and candidate details, subject to FR-2/FR-3 dedup rules.

**Consequences (testable):**
- Submission is rejected (per FR-2) if the candidate is already in the pipeline for that role.
- Submitted candidate is tagged with Source = `agency` and the specific Agency identity.

**Feature-specific NFRs:**
- An Agency must never be able to see another Agency's submissions, candidates, or activity for the same Role, even though they share a Role ID.

### 5.3 Internal HR Visibility & Per-Role Dashboard

**Description:** Internal HR's control-tower view — every candidate for a role, regardless of source, with a per-role dashboard summarizing pipeline state.

**Functional Requirements:**

#### FR-8: Full candidate visibility with source tagging `[Must]`
Internal HR can see all Candidates submitted against any Role, tagged with Source (internal-hr, employee-referral, or agency + which agency). Realizes UJ-2.

#### FR-9: Per-role dashboard `[Must]`
Internal HR and the Hiring Manager can view a per-role dashboard showing all Candidates and their current Interview Level/status at a glance. Realizes UJ-2, UJ-3.

**Consequences (testable):**
- Dashboard reflects the latest Candidate status on page load; v1 does not require real-time push (e.g., websockets) — a page refresh is sufficient.

#### FR-10: Audience-scoped dashboard detail `[Should]`
The per-role dashboard shows different detail by audience: Internal HR sees Source, Agency identity, and Agency-related detail; the Hiring Manager sees Candidate identity and pipeline status only, not Agency-specific commercial detail.

**Consequences (testable):**
- A Hiring Manager viewing the dashboard cannot see which Agency submitted a given candidate, or that Agency's commercial/fee terms (fee terms are out of scope for v1 regardless — see §6 — but the visibility boundary is enforced now for when they exist).

### 5.4 Hiring Manager Pipeline Configuration

**Description:** The Hiring Manager defines how many interview levels a role requires and who's approved to interview at each — this structure becomes the pipeline every candidate for that role moves through.

**Functional Requirements:**

#### FR-11: Define interview levels per role `[Must]`
The Hiring Manager can set the number and names of Interview Levels for a Role (e.g., Screen, Technical, Final). Realizes UJ-3.

**Consequences (testable):**
- Every Candidate under that Role progresses through the same defined levels, in order.
- Levels can be defined once at role setup; `[ASSUMPTION]` mid-pipeline editing of levels (e.g. adding a level after candidates are already in progress) is out of scope for v1 — see Open Questions.

#### FR-12: Interviewer pools per level `[Should]`
The Hiring Manager can assign an Interviewer Pool (one or more approved interviewers) to each Interview Level.

**Consequences (testable):**
- When scheduling an interview for a candidate at a given level (FR-13), only interviewers from that level's pool are selectable.
- An Interview Level cannot be activated for scheduling until it has at least one interviewer in its pool — prevents candidates from stalling at a level with no one available to interview them.

#### FR-13: Full candidate visibility with submitter identity `[Must]`
The Hiring Manager can see all Candidates for their Role across all Sources, including who submitted each one (Internal HR, specific Agency, or referring employee). Realizes UJ-3.

### 5.5 Interview Scheduling & Notifications

**Description:** Scheduling interviews, keeping the Hiring Manager informed, and closing the loop with candidates and submitters — without giving candidates platform access.

**Functional Requirements:**

#### FR-14: Schedule interviews in-app `[Must]`
Internal HR or an Agency Recruiter can schedule an interview for a Candidate at their current Interview Level, selecting an interviewer from that level's Interviewer Pool. Realizes UJ-3.

**Consequences (testable):**
- Scheduling is blocked if it would double-book the selected interviewer or the Candidate against another already-scheduled interview in an overlapping slot.

#### FR-15: Hiring manager notified on interview logged `[Should]`
The Hiring Manager is notified when an interview is scheduled/logged for a Candidate in their Role, including the interviewer's identity and time. Realizes UJ-3.

**Consequences (testable):**
- Notification is delivered in-app/dashboard (not email — the Hiring Manager is an internal SSO user; email in this PRD is reserved for the candidate-facing channel in FR-16).
- The same notification fires again if the interview is later rescheduled or cancelled, not only on initial scheduling — the Hiring Manager should never be working from a stale time.

#### FR-16: Candidate email for interview logistics `[Must]`
The system sends interview logistics (time, place/link) directly to the Candidate by email once an interview is scheduled.

**Consequences (testable):**
- This is the one candidate-facing communication in v1; it contains logistics only, not pipeline status.
- If the interview is rescheduled or cancelled after the original email was sent, an updated or cancellation email is sent to the Candidate — they are never left with only the stale original time.
- `[ASSUMPTION]` Delivery-failure handling (bounce, bad address) is not defined for v1 beyond best-effort send — see Open Questions.

#### FR-17: Status visibility for submitters via portal `[Must]`
Agency Recruiters and employee referrers see their submitted Candidate's current status via the portal (not pushed by email).

**Consequences (testable):**
- No email is sent to the submitter on every status change; status is pull, not push, in v1.
- Employee referrers are internal org members, not external partners — they authenticate into this portal view via the same company SSO used by Internal HR/Hiring Managers (see Constraints and Guardrails). No separate referrer onboarding flow exists or is needed.

**Feature-specific NFRs:**
- Candidate email delivery must be reliable enough that a missed interview invite is not attributable to the platform. `[ASSUMPTION]` no specific deliverability SLA defined — see Open Questions.

### 5.6 Interview Feedback & Pipeline Advancement

**Description:** Closes the loop the pipeline structure (§5.4) otherwise leaves open: how a Candidate actually moves from one Interview Level to the next. The interviewer records structured feedback; the Hiring Manager — not an automatic rule — decides whether the Candidate advances.

**Functional Requirements:**

#### FR-23: Interviewer submits structured feedback `[Must]`
The interviewer assigned to a scheduled interview (FR-14) submits feedback: ratings for **Communication**, **Technical**, and **Enthusiasm**; a free-text detail section; and a verdict of **No Hire**, **Weak Hire**, **Good Hire**, or **Must Hire**.

**Consequences (testable):**
- Only the interviewer assigned to that specific scheduled interview can submit feedback for it.
- Feedback is immutable once submitted, consistent with the audit-immutability principle already applied to FR-4.
- `[ASSUMPTION]` Communication/Technical/Enthusiasm ratings use a 1–5 scale — no scale was specified by the stakeholder.

#### FR-24: Hiring Manager notified of submitted feedback `[Must]`
The Hiring Manager is notified when feedback is submitted for a Candidate in their Role, seeing the interviewer's identity, all three ratings, the free-text detail, and the verdict.

**Consequences (testable):**
- Notification is delivered in-app/dashboard, matching FR-15's channel.
- `[ASSUMPTION]` Feedback content (ratings, free text, verdict) is visible to Internal HR and the Hiring Manager only — never to the submitting Agency, referrer, or candidate — following the same audience-scoping principle as FR-10.

#### FR-25: Hiring Manager advances or rejects candidate `[Must]`
Using the submitted feedback as input — not an automatic rule — the Hiring Manager decides whether the Candidate proceeds to the next Interview Level or is rejected. Realizes UJ-3.

**Consequences (testable):**
- If advanced and a next Interview Level exists, the Candidate becomes schedulable at that level (FR-14).
- If advanced at the final Interview Level, the Candidate is offer-ready, feeding the Position Record flow (FR-19).
- If not advanced, the Candidate's status becomes `Rejected`, visible on the per-role dashboard (FR-9) and to their submitter via FR-17.
- Candidate status values: see Glossary (Candidate Status) and FR-18, which shares the same vocabulary for requisition-close handling.

### 5.7 Requisition Lifecycle & Position Records

**Description:** Requisitions open and close explicitly; a closed-and-filled requisition becomes a persistent position record instead of disappearing.

**Functional Requirements:**

#### FR-18: Open and close requisitions `[Must]`
Internal HR can open a new requisition and close it (filled or cancelled). Realizes UJ-4.

**Consequences (testable):**
- Closing a Requisition never deletes Candidate records; every in-flight (`Active`) Candidate is transitioned to a terminal status, never left dangling.
- `[ASSUMPTION]` Closing as **filled**: the hired Candidate moves to `Hired` (feeds FR-19); every other in-flight Candidate for that Role ID moves to `Rejected (role filled)`, visible to their submitter via FR-17.
- `[ASSUMPTION]` Closing as **cancelled**: every in-flight Candidate for that Role ID moves to `Withdrawn (requisition cancelled)`, visible to their submitter via FR-17.

#### FR-19: Position record on fill `[Should]`
When a requisition closes as filled, it converts into a Position Record tied to the hired employee. Realizes UJ-4.

**Consequences (testable):**
- If the position later becomes vacant again, reopening it is linked to the existing Position Record rather than starting as an unrelated new Role ID.
- `[ASSUMPTION]` The exact reopen mechanism (same Role ID reactivated vs. new Role ID linked to the old Position Record) is left to architecture — see Open Questions.

### 5.8 Recruitment Health Reporting

**Description:** A rolled-up signal of recruitment health, aggregated bottoms-up through the org hierarchy so leadership doesn't have to chase every team individually.

**Functional Requirements:**

#### FR-20: Recruitment health metrics per team `[Should]`
The system computes time-to-fill, aging-requisition count, pipeline volume per role, and offer-accept rate per team. Realizes UJ-4.

**Consequences (testable):**
- `[ASSUMPTION]` A Requisition counts as "aging" once open more than 45 days with no offer extended — no threshold was specified by the stakeholder; revisit once real time-to-fill data exists (see §8 SM-1).
- A team with zero requisitions or zero completed hires in the reporting period shows an explicit "no data" state for offer-accept rate and time-to-fill, never a misleading 0% or divide-by-zero.

#### FR-21: Bottoms-up rollup for leadership `[Should]`
Managers-of-managers can view recruitment health aggregated from all teams under them in the org hierarchy. Realizes UJ-4.

**Consequences (testable):**
- A leader sees their org's rollup without needing to individually open each team's dashboard.

**Notes:** *(fast-follow, not MVP-blocking)*
- `[NON-GOAL for MVP]` Automatic surfacing/alerting of aging requisitions past a threshold is deferred — v1 leadership rollup is a pull view, not push alerts. See §7.

### 5.9 Agency Performance Scorecard

**Description:** Gives each agency a transparent view of their own conversion performance — referred vs. progressed vs. joined — building trust in the fairness of the dedup/credit system.

**Functional Requirements:**

#### FR-22: Per-agency scorecard `[Should]`
An Agency Recruiter can see their own Agency's funnel: candidates referred, how many progressed through each Interview Level, and how many joined.

**Consequences (testable):**
- Scorecard is scoped to the viewing Agency's own data only — no cross-agency comparison exposed in v1.

**Notes:**
- `[NON-GOAL for MVP]` Using the scorecard's "joined" event to automatically trigger a placement-fee/invoice event is deferred — v1 scorecard is informational only, no finance/payment integration. See §7 and `addendum.md`.

## 6. Non-Goals (Explicit)

- **No candidate-facing product.** Candidates never log in, never see status in-app, and never receive anything beyond interview-logistics email (FR-16). This is a deliberate, explicit boundary, not an oversight.
- Not a general-purpose Applicant Tracking System (ATS) or job board — no public job postings, no candidate self-registration, no open-market sourcing.
- Not a payroll or full HRIS system. The Position Record (FR-19) is a lightweight link between a filled requisition and an employee, not a system of record for compensation, benefits, or performance.
- Not a finance/invoicing system in v1 — the Agency Scorecard (FR-22) does not trigger payments (see §7).
- No self-service agency registration — agencies are onboarded by internal HR (see §5.2, and the Integration and Dependencies subsection under Constraints and Guardrails), not by signing themselves up.

## 7. Out of Scope for MVP

# Addendum — Hiring Ascent PRD

Depth and technical detail that doesn't belong in the PRD narrative but is worth preserving for the teams that pick this up next (architecture, downstream v1.1/v2 planning). Companion to `prd.md` in this same folder — section numbers below (e.g. "PRD §7") refer to that document.

## Duplicate/near-duplicate submission handling — deferred (PRD §7)

Two related mechanisms were considered for strengthening v1's exact-match dedup and were explicitly deferred, not rejected:

### Fuzzy-match dedup

v1 dedup (FR-2) is exact-match only: email, phone, resume-hash. When this is revisited, candidate mechanisms discussed:
- Name + phone variant normalization (formatting differences, country codes, nicknames).
- Resume-content similarity scoring (structural/text similarity, not just hash-identical files).
- LinkedIn URL as a secondary identity anchor.

None of these were scoped to a specific algorithm or threshold — that's an architecture-stage decision, not a PRD commitment. Worth flagging: fuzzy matching introduces false-positive risk (blocking two genuinely different people who happen to share a common name), which the exact-match v1 approach avoids entirely. Any fuzzy-match design should include a manual-override path for HR.

### Grace-window manual review

Idea explored: submissions landing within a short window of each other (hours, not days) route to manual HR review instead of automatic first-timestamp-wins. Not scoped for v1 because it adds a manual-adjudication workflow (queue, reviewer UI, SLA on review time) that the org hasn't asked for yet — v1's strict first-timestamp-wins + visible timestamp (FR-4) was judged sufficient to start.

## Agency scorecard as payment trigger (deferred, PRD §5.9 / §7)

The idea: a candidate reaching "joined" in the Agency Scorecard funnel (FR-22) could automatically fire a placement-fee/invoice event, rather than being purely informational. This was explicitly called out as attractive but out of scope for v1 because it implies a finance/invoicing system integration (or build) that hasn't been scoped — payment terms, invoice generation, dispute-on-payment handling, etc. are all open questions. If pursued later, this likely needs its own mini-PRD or a finance-stakeholder-driven requirements pass rather than being bolted onto this one.

## Position Record reopen mechanism (PRD Open Question 7)

Two shapes were implicit in the brainstorm but not decided:
1. The same Role ID gets reactivated when the seat opens again (simpler, but blurs "requisition" and "position" into one entity).
2. A new Role ID is created for the reopened search, linked to the existing Position Record (cleaner separation between "a specific hiring event" and "a seat's history," but requires an explicit link/history model).
Recommend that architecture make this call — it has real data-model implications for how headcount/turnover reporting eventually gets built.

The thesis is stated once and never re-argued: dedup at the point of submission is called out as having "surfaced independently across three separate design discussions and is treated as the non-negotiable core the rest of the system depends on" (§4.1), and everything else — Must/Should tags, the counter-metrics, the fuzzy-match deferral — traces back to protecting that core. Counter-metrics are a genuine strength: SM-C1 and SM-C2 (§7) explicitly name the metric-gaming failure mode ("Time-to-fill should not improve by hiring managers cutting interview levels to game the metric") rather than listing SMs in isolation. This is not a backlog with headings — the MVP scope logic (§6.1) is legible as "protect the credit/trust system first, add visibility/reporting second."

## Done-ness clarity — adequate

Most FRs carry a testable "Consequences" block that would let an engineer write acceptance tests directly (FR-1 through FR-4, FR-5, FR-7, FR-9 through FR-12, FR-16, FR-17, FR-19, FR-21, FR-22 all have one). But seven FRs have none: **FR-6, FR-8, FR-13, FR-14, FR-15, FR-18, FR-20**. For some (FR-6 "view the full JD," FR-14 "schedule interviews in-app") the FR sentence itself is close to self-testing, but for others the gap is load-bearing.

### Findings
- **high** FR-18 (Open and close requisitions, `[Must]`, §4.6) has no consequences block, and its most consequential behavior — what happens to candidates mid-pipeline when a requisition closes or is cancelled — is left to Open Question 7 ("What happens to in-flight candidates (mid-pipeline) if a requisition is closed or cancelled before completion?") with no assumption offered in the interim. This is a Must-tagged FR with an unresolved core behavior, not a Should-tagged edge case. *Fix:* add a consequences block and either answer the in-flight-candidate question or tag it `[ASSUMPTION]` with a stated default (e.g., "candidates in-flight are marked withdrawn, not deleted") so FR-18 is buildable without a mid-sprint PM interrupt.
- **medium** FR-20 (Recruitment health metrics, `[Should]`, §4.7) defines "aging-requisition count" as one of its four computed metrics but never defines what "aging" means — no day threshold anywhere in the FR, its consequences (absent), the Glossary (§3, "Recruitment Health" entry lists the metric names but not thresholds), or the Non-Goal callout that references it ("Automatic surfacing/alerting of aging requisitions past a threshold," §4.7 Notes). The term is used three times across the document without ever being bounded. *Fix:* define the aging threshold (even as an `[ASSUMPTION]`, e.g., "requisitions open >45 days with no offer") so FR-20 and its dependent Non-Goal are both computable.
- **medium** FR-15 (Hiring manager notified on interview logged, `[Should]`, §4.5) specifies content ("interviewer's identity and time") but not delivery channel — email, in-app, both? FR-16 explicitly resolves this question for candidate-facing communication ("The system sends interview logistics... directly to the Candidate by email") but FR-15 doesn't extend the same clarity to the hiring-manager notification, and no consequences block exists to fill the gap. *Fix:* state the channel explicitly, or tag it `[ASSUMPTION]` alongside the existing email-deliverability assumption in §4.5.
- **low** FR-6, FR-8, FR-13 lack consequences blocks but their FR statements are largely self-testable as written (visibility and JD-review claims already read as verifiable conditions). Flagging for consistency with the rest of §4, not because they're ambiguous. *Fix:* low priority — add one-line consequences for uniformity if the section is revised for other reasons.

Non-Goals (§5) do real work rather than listing the obvious — "Not a payroll or full HRIS system. The Position Record (FR-19) is a lightweight link... not a system of record for compensation, benefits, or performance" draws a boundary a reader could otherwise assume away. `[NON-GOAL for MVP]` and `[ASSUMPTION]` tags are used throughout (§4.7, §4.8, §6.2, §9) and de-scoping is argued, not silent — the addendum gives the actual reasoning for deferring fuzzy-match, grace-window review, and the payment-trigger, including the false-positive risk trade-off for fuzzy matching. Open-items density (9 Open Questions, 7 indexed assumptions, 3 `[NOTE FOR PM]` callouts) is proportionate for a platform PRD that explicitly defers SSO/email vendor and data-retention decisions to Integration — these read as genuinely unresolved external dependencies, not scope avoidance.

## Downstream usability — adequate

The Glossary (§3) is genuinely used — FR text consistently says "Role ID," "Source," "Interview Level" rather than drifting into synonyms, and ID sequences (FR-1–FR-22, UJ-1–UJ-4, SM-1–SM-4/SM-C1–SM-C2) are contiguous with no gaps or duplicates.

### Findings
- **medium** UJ-4's protagonist is unnamed (§2.3): "A director two levels above Marcus, reviewing hiring health for the quarter" — every other UJ has a named protagonist (Amara, Priya, Marcus) carrying context inline; UJ-4 breaks the pattern the rubric calls load-bearing for downstream extraction (a UX/architecture reader can't refer back to "the director" the way they can to "Marcus"). *Fix:* name the persona (e.g., "Diane") for consistency with UJ-1–UJ-3.
- **low** The Glossary conflates two distinct mechanisms into one entry: "**Dedup / Pre-Check** — The identity-matching process... that prevents duplicate Candidate Submissions" (§3). - **low** §5's cross-reference is unclear: "agencies are onboarded by internal HR (see §4.2 access model in Constraints below)" conflates §4.2 (Agency Access & Candidate Submission) with the separate "Constraints and Guardrails" section at the document's end — a reader following the link doesn't know which section is being pointed to. *Fix:* cite them as two separate references, e.g., "(see §4.2, and the Integration and Dependencies subsection under Constraints and Guardrails)."

This is correctly shaped as a multi-stakeholder B2B-adjacent internal platform: UJs with named protagonists are load-bearing here (agencies are external partner organizations with their own incentives, so "Amara's afternoon" and "Priya's dispute" are doing real work, not decoration), and the PRD correctly avoids over-formalizing a single-operator tool with unnecessary UX narrative. ### 2. MOVE - Cross-Cutting NFRs and Constraints and Guardrails
**Rationale:** Both sections are placed last (positions 11–12 of 12) despite being forward-referenced multiple times from inside §4 — FR-2 and FR-4 both say "See Cross-Cutting NFRs," FR-17 says "see Constraints and Guardrails," and §6.1 says "see §Constraints." ### 3. MOVE - MVP scope summary (§6.1 In Scope) surfaced earlier
**Rationale:** The closest thing this PRD has to a Pyramid "conclusion/recommendation" — what actually ships in v1 — doesn't appear until §6, roughly 3,700 words (two-thirds of the way) into the document, after Target User, Glossary, and the full 2,400-word Features section. **Impact:** ~0 words (reorder only); move §6.1's In Scope (v1) Must/Should list to immediately after §1 Vision, ahead of §2 Target User — gives the reader the scope decision before the supporting detail, consistent with the Pyramid model's top-down rule.

**Rationale:** Three of the five Cross-Cutting NFRs bullets are near-verbatim restatements of Feature-specific NFRs/consequences already stated in §4: "Dedup must be synchronous and immutable" duplicates §4.1's Feature-specific NFR ("Dedup check must complete synchronously…") and FR-2/FR-4's consequences; "Submission timestamps are authoritative and server-side" duplicates FR-2's and FR-4's consequence bullets; "Access control is the load-bearing security property" duplicates FR-5's consequence and FR-7's Feature-specific NFR. **Rationale:** "Candidate status values in v1: `Active`, `Rejected`, `Withdrawn`, `Hired`" appears verbatim three times: once as the canonical Glossary definition (§3, cross-referencing FR-18 and FR-25 already), once in FR-18's consequences, and once again in FR-25's consequences — which even explicitly says "shared with FR-18's requisition-close handling" right before restating the full list anyway.
